claims.text: Nanoscale precipitates form in refractory high-entropy alloys during processing.
The formation and distribution of nanoscale precipitates govern the high-temperature mechanical behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The formation and distribution of nanoscale precipitates govern the thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Dislocation pinning and internal-stress redistribution improve strength retention at elevated temperatures.
Dislocation pinning and internal-stress redistribution modify the elevated-temperature elastic response.
A solutionizing-plus-aging heat treatment will promote nanoscale precipitation relative to an as-cast or solutionized control.
Extended solutionizing followed by quenching can minimize precipitate formation.
Precipitate-induced inhibition of dislocation motion delays high-temperature softening.
Precipitate-induced local stress fields change the rate at which elastic modulus decreases with temperature.
Sluggish diffusion inherent to refractory high-entropy alloys stabilizes the beneficial precipitate-containing microstructure at high temperature.
High mixing entropy inherent to refractory high-entropy alloys stabilizes the beneficial precipitate-containing microstructure at high temperature.
The precipitate-rich heat-treated alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength than the precipitate-poor baseline.
The precipitate-rich heat-treated alloy will have higher high-temperature flow strength than the precipitate-poor baseline.
The precipitate-rich heat-treated alloy will show slower degradation of thermoelastic stiffness with increasing temperature, or potentially increased effective stiffness.
The magnitude of the predicted improvements depends on precipitate size, volume fraction, and spatial distribution.
Precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution are sensitive to the heat-treatment parameters.
